judge: Maya — product designer, consent-forward / women-first products (Bumble lens: who moves first, who holds control, how exposure is managed, whether defaults protect her, whether her feedback is design input)
first_five_minutes:
Minute 0 — /login. The page is genuinely beautiful: Jane Eyre's "I am no bird; and no net ensnares me," and "A little more room to be the author." Then, directly under the password field she reads `login-form.tsx:56`: "Private access, by invitation. Your workspace owner can help with access or a password reset." Her first sentence about her own workspace is that someone else holds her keys. She signs in with credentials Michael gave her.

Minute 1 — she lands on `/`. The heading says "Welcome home, Cassandra." The sidebar directly to its left says "Kira Stanley · Author workspace." The chip at the bottom of the sidebar says her email and, underneath, "Human in command" (`app-shell.tsx:224`) — a label she did not choose, on a workspace where she is an Editor. Nothing anywhere explains that Kira and Cassandra are the same woman, so for the first minute she is reasonably unsure whether she is looking at her own account or Kira Stanley's.

Minute 2 — "Start with one small thing." Three steps. Step two is "Add to your **shared** desk" (`getting-started.tsx:85`) and the subtitle says "Counts include starter briefs and work saved by everyone in this workspace" (`getting-started.tsx:118`). The desk with her name on it is a shared desk. The four counters below read 08 / 00 / 00 / 00. Her workspace is empty and, at the same time, communal.

Minute 3 — first click, almost certainly "Open your books" (step 01, the only non-empty thing). `/universe` opens with "Your words become Kira's reference. Add a manuscript. **Kira reads it** in small steps, saves what it learns" (`connected-library.tsx:67`). Her pen name is now the name of the machine. She opens *Assassin's Refusal*.

Minute 4 — the book page: "**Let Kira get to know this book.**" A file picker, an unchecked permission box, and a gold "Upload & let Kira read" button. The consent is real and opt-in — good. But nowhere on that card does it say where the file is stored, for how long, that every editor and viewer Michael grants can read the extracted passages and spoilers, or how she takes it back. There is no take-it-back: no delete endpoint exists anywhere in `app/api/manuscripts/*`. If she is the kind of author who does not hand a draft to anyone, she closes the panel here.

Minute 5 — if she instead clicks "Marketing Plans," the very first line under "Your plans" is `plans-page.tsx:47`: "Draft → **owner review** → active tasks → results." Before she has written a single word of a plan for her own books, the product has told her the workflow ends at someone else's desk. If she builds one anyway, `plans-page.tsx:104` will tell her by name: "Michael can review this plan and activate its tasks. You can keep exploring while it awaits review."

Net: the craft and the honesty land immediately and well. The authority does not. Within five minutes she has been told three times, in three different rooms, that the workspace built for her is governed by someone else — and she has been offered her manuscript-sharing decision without being told how to reverse it.

scores.verdict: The product repeatedly puts a named man between Cassy and her own business. She can build a marketing plan for her own books but cannot approve or activate it; the gate is announced before she starts and again by Michael's first name when she hits it. Her workspace's flagship creative exercise is 'Start an idea for Michael.' Her sign-in page tells her the owner controls her password. This is the largest gap against the brief, and most of it is fixable in code even before the role question is settled.

scores.verdict: Draft protection is excellent and clearly loved: unfinished-idea choice dialogs, a sign-out confirmation, a beforeunload guard, optimistic-concurrency checks, and 'your text is still here' on every failure. But the one truly irreversible thing in the product — uploading her manuscript and having it read, chunked, quoted and indexed — has no undo at all. There is no DELETE route under app/api/manuscripts/* and no remove control in the UI. An experiment she cannot reverse is not a safe experiment.

scores.verdict: The self-explanation machinery is genuinely strong — ContextHelp on four pages, the Guide dialog, Getting Started, honest demo/manual/live labelling. 'Private to your workspace' will be read as 'private to me'; it actually means readable by everyone the owner grants access to.

top_findings.title: Her manuscript has no exit: no delete, no retention terms, no stated audience
top_findings.problem: The permission checkbox is opt-in and well written, but there is no DELETE route under app/api/manuscripts/* and no remove control in any component — I grepped for both. Once she uploads an unpublished draft, the file, its chunks, the extracted characters, spoiler-flagged plot facts and the search index are permanent. She is also never told where it is stored, for how long, or that every editor and viewer the owner grants can read the passages; connected-library.tsx:67 says only 'Private to your workspace', which a person reads as 'private to me'.
top_findings.proposed_change: Add DELETE app/api/manuscripts/[id] plus a caller-scoped RPC that removes the manuscript, its chunks and its derived knowledge under the existing RLS pattern. Surface it as 'Remove this version' on each manuscript-history row and 'Remove this manuscript and everything read from it' on the progress card, behind a typed confirmation naming exactly what goes and what stays. Beside the consent checkbox add three lines: destination (named provider/model), retention (until she removes it), audience (workspace members with access, linking /access). Change connected-library.tsx:67 to state that audience honestly.

top_findings.title: Michael gates her marketing plans by name, and the app says so before she starts
top_findings.problem: The owner-review card renders only for role === 'owner' (line 103), so as an Editor Cassy can build a plan for her own books, spend AI credits generating it, and then hit a hardcoded sentence naming her best friend as the person who decides. The gate is also the first thing the page teaches: line 47 leads with 'Draft → owner review → active tasks → results.' She cannot withdraw a plan from review, cannot activate her own dated tasks, and is told to 'keep exploring while it awaits review.'
top_findings.proposed_change: Code tonight: derive the reviewer from the access record rather than hardcoding 'Michael'; rewrite line 104 to state what she can still do; add explicit 'Ask for review' / 'Withdraw from review' controls so entering review is her move; rewrite line 47 to lead with her actions and mention the sign-off second. Note tests/e2e-connected/plans.spec.ts:26 asserts the heading 'Needs owner review' — that label can stay while the surrounding framing changes.
top_findings.owner_decision_needed: Should Cassy be Owner rather than Editor, or should plan approval become an editor capability with owner notification? The gate's existence is Michael's call; its framing is entirely code. He should also decide whether he is comfortable being named in the UI as the approver of her marketing.

top_findings.title: Her pen name is the name of the machine that reads her manuscript
top_findings.problem: 'Your words become Kira's reference. Add a manuscript. Kira reads it in small steps, saves what it learns.' Also 'Let Kira get to know this book' (connected-book-detail.tsx:118), 'What Kira learned' (line 130), 'Kira will keep reading in the background' (line 61), 'explore what Kira learned' (connected-home.tsx:161). The brief's stated concept is that Kira is her creative self and the workspace carries the business. The product has instead assigned her author identity to the AI consuming her drafts — while the sidebar shows 'Kira Stanley · Author workspace' and the greeting says 'Cassandra', with nothing explaining these are one woman.
top_findings.proposed_change: Replace every personified 'Kira' denoting the AI with 'this workspace' / 'your reference library' / passive voice: connected-library.tsx:67, connected-book-detail.tsx:61, 118, 125, 130, connected-home.tsx:161. Keep 'KIRA OS' as the product name and 'Kira Stanley' as her byline. Separately add the connective line in the sidebar identity block (app-shell.tsx:109): 'Kira Stanley' / 'Cassandra's author workspace'.

top_findings.title: 'The minions are working. Go write. 🖤' — condescending and false
top_findings.problem: The demo empty state on both Mission Control and the Desk (desk-page.tsx:110) tells her an invisible team is working on her behalf. Two cards down on the same page, agent-status.tsx:34-43 lists every specialist as 'Not connected' with status IDLE. It is a fake autonomous-status claim (AGENTS.md rule 2) delivered in a pat-on-the-head register. Adjacent: 'The coven is here.' as the heading over her follower count (line 143), 'Take your seat' as the CTA for her own desk (line 100), and 'Human in command' as her sidebar role label (app-shell.tsx:224).
top_findings.proposed_change: mission-control.tsx:94 and desk-page.tsx:110 → 'Nothing waiting. Add an idea whenever one turns up.' mission-control.tsx:143 → 'The readers who found you.' mission-control.tsx:100 → 'Open your desk'. app-shell.tsx:224 → render the actual role from useWorkspace(). No e2e test pins any of these four strings — I grepped tests/ for 'minions', 'coven', 'Take your seat' and 'Human in command' and found nothing. The nearby demo-home heading 'Good afternoon, Cassandra.' IS pinned by tests/e2e/workspace.spec.ts:11; leave it alone.

top_findings.title: The front door tells her the owner holds her keys
top_findings.problem: Under the password field on the sign-in page: 'Private access, by invitation. Your workspace owner can help with access or a password reset.' This is the first sentence the app's actual user reads about her own workspace, and it casts her as a guest with a chaperone. Reinforced at settings-page.tsx:119 ('Your workspace owner controls access'), access-page.tsx:17 ('Only the owner can manage access'), and app/login/page.tsx:78 ('Ask your workspace owner for access').
top_findings.proposed_change: login-form.tsx:56 → 'Private access. Only accounts added to this workspace can sign in.' Put recovery on its own smaller line; if owner-mediated reset is genuinely the only path today, say so plainly rather than folding it into the welcome. settings-page.tsx:119 → lead with capability. access-page.tsx:17 → 'You can create and edit briefs, approve or reject them, save lessons, and export everything. Managing who else has access is the owner's role.'

top_findings.title: Her creative workshop's flagship exercise is 'Start an idea for Michael'
top_findings.problem: The most prominent affordance on Learn & Create — above the recipe grid, in its own callout — is 'Have something in mind for Michael?' / 'Start an idea for Michael'. The backing starter (lib/data/agent-recipes.ts:73-78) reads 'Help me create a new business-agent idea for Michael that we can discuss together… I will decide whether to share it.' The Studio's agent-design starter (studio-page.tsx:25) is the same text. The one feature in her workspace framed around a named person is framed around the man who built it.
top_findings.proposed_change: Reframe as hers with a shareable output: callout 'Shaping an idea to hand to someone?', button 'Start an idea to share', and a neutral michaelAgentStarter whose success line keeps 'I decide whether to share it.' Pinned copy: tests/e2e-connected/new-features.spec.ts:37 asserts the button name, and tests/agent-recipes.test.ts:31-35 asserts the blueprint title contains 'Michael' and the brief contains 'does not run an agent or send anything to Michael'. Update both in the same change; the guarantee should survive as 'does not send anything to anyone'.
top_findings.owner_decision_needed: Michael may have added this deliberately as a channel for Cassy to send him requests. If so, keep the capability but rename it so her workshop is not organised around him — and decide whether it belongs on Learn & Create at all versus as a share action on any saved blueprint.

top_findings.title: Marketing Plans drops out of the design system on the app's highest-stakes form
top_findings.problem: PlanForm and PlanDetail use raw <input>, <textarea> and <select> elements throughout (lines 64-71, 106) while every other surface uses the Input/Textarea components and .form-label. In cdesktop-plans.png the result is visibly a cruder product than the desk or library — and it is the page where she sets budget, dates and measurable goals.
top_findings.proposed_change: Swap the native controls for the existing Input, Textarea and .access-role-select styling, and apply form-label to the labels. While in there, fix the Progress select's Label-in-Name problem at line 101 by rendering the task title as visually-hidden text inside the visible 'Progress' label.

top_findings.title: Nav sublabels — the only thing decoding the internal vocabulary — are hidden from screen readers
top_findings.problem: Every explanatory <small> in the sidebar carries aria-hidden="true" (lines 134, 151, 166), and the links carry aria-label={title}. A screen-reader user hears 'Mission Control', 'The Universe', 'Briefings', 'The Hunt', 'The Vault' with none of 'Your day at a glance', 'Your books & their details', 'Evidence & recommendations to review'. The 'Coming later' items (line 186) have no descriptions at all for anyone.
top_findings.proposed_change: Drop aria-hidden from the three <small> elements and remove the now-redundant aria-label={title} so the accessible name is title + description (or set aria-label to `${title}. ${description}`). Give the 'Coming later' entries the one-line descriptions that already exist in the modules map in app/[module]/page.tsx. Separately, extend the existing axe sweep to /plans, /studio, /learn, /connections and /access.

what_works: Draft protection is the best thing in this product and must not be touched. The unfinished-idea choice dialog (manual-review-form.tsx:131-161) with 'Nothing changes until you choose', the same pattern on book-details-brief.tsx:24 and book-detail.tsx:214-222, the sign-out confirmation that names exactly what is discarded (app-shell.tsx:415-429), the beforeunload guard (demo-store.tsx:471-476), and clearScratchpad's refusal to erase words typed after a submission (demo-store.tsx:250-254).

Every failure message tells her where her words are: 'Your idea could not be saved. Your text is still here' (manual-review-form.tsx:99), 'Your manuscript is unchanged; please try again' (book-knowledge.tsx:82), 'Your unfinished work is still here' (app-shell.tsx:270), 'The book could not be saved. Your entries are still here' (connected-library.tsx:38). Keep this convention on any new error string.

Optimistic-concurrency honesty on the approval card: changedSinceOpening (approval-card.tsx:41) plus the alert at line 210 — 'This brief changed while you were reviewing it. Cancel, read the latest version, then choose your next step.' A shared desk needs exactly this and most products skip it.

Spoiler controls that default closed and count what they are hiding (book-knowledge.tsx:89), the separate opt-in before manuscript search (connected-book-detail.tsx:135), and the source-passage dialog's warning that the text may contain spoilers and is not approved marketing copy (line 138).

Epistemic honesty in the knowledge panel: 'Findings with quotations that cannot be matched exactly to the manuscript are omitted. A matching quotation does not guarantee that the interpretation is correct' (connected-book-detail.tsx:131), the per-item 'Manuscript-supported · unreviewed' vs 'Interpretation · verify with source' tag (book-knowledge.tsx:102), and 'this is not an approved character bible'. Do not soften any of it.

Provenance and status labelling throughout: DemoBadge, 'NEEDS VERIFICATION', 'MANUAL SNAPSHOT', 'Snapshot date unknown · Not live' (mission-control.tsx:158), 'No live sources were queried' (demo-store.tsx:355), 'it does not retrain a model' (approval-card.tsx:186), per-question model cost (studio-page.tsx:203), and 'Refreshing does not connect accounts or purchase credits' (setup-status.tsx:79).

Focus management after dialogs is unusually thorough and easy to break in a refactor: onCloseAutoFocus returning focus to the triggering button, falling back to the Reviewed tab when the trigger unmounts (approval-card.tsx:170-175); keepWorkingRef focus on the sign-out dialog; statusRef focus after every access mutation (access-page.tsx:96).

The literary quote card (daily-quote.tsx, lib/data/inspiration.ts:129-165) — real primary sources, exact excerpt boundaries, Gutenberg links, a note on where the line sits in the book, and Jane Eyre's 'I am no bird' as the default. This is the warmest, most adult thing in the interface and it is the right register for the whole product.

The inspiration ideas (lib/data/inspiration.ts:19-107) are genuinely respectful: they ask her questions rather than telling her findings, every brief draft ends with a verification step, and none of them invent a fact about her books.
The creative firewall table in Settings (settings-page.tsx:74-91) with the honest footnote that 'Allowed describes policy permission, not an implemented feature'.
The NotebookLM bridge (connections-page.tsx:132-139): a textarea that explicitly is not saved or sent, copying only what she selects. A model for how to build an integration that does not overreach.

Accessibility foundations: skip link, reduced-motion block (globals.css:2689), labelled controls, live regions on save state, the aria-roledescription carousel with arrow-key support and an sr-only instructions line (inspiration-shelf.tsx:49-50), and axe-clean wcag21aa on /, /universe, /desk and /settings.
